summary: Astronauts lose muscle strength in space because microgravity removes the load that normally keeps their muscles working. NASA data show lower-body muscle size and strength dropping by about 10–15% on missions lasting from two weeks to six months. Our solution, the Muscle Health Check, is a simple monitoring tool that tracks this loss in orbit. Once a week, in a five-minute test, the astronaut squeezes a handgrip dynamometer three times while an EMG sensor on the forearm records the muscle’s electrical signals. The device compares the best result with the astronaut’s own pre-launch baseline and shows a color: green (stable, keep the plan), yellow (declining, add exercise and retest), or red (below the safe margin, so a flight surgeon reviews and may consider returning to Earth).
details:
The Muscle Health Check is a health monitoring system that tracks muscle loss in astronauts during space missions and turns the results into a clear decision. In microgravity, muscles stop working against gravity, so postural muscles in the calves, thighs, and back shrink and weaken. NASA data show lower-body muscle size and strength dropping by about 10–15% on ISS missions lasting from two weeks to six months. Our system works through a simple five-minute weekly routine:

  1. Baseline: Before launch, we record the astronaut’s grip force and EMG signal.
  2. Weekly test: The astronaut squeezes a handgrip dynamometer three times with EMG sensors on the forearm. The dynamometer measures maximum grip force, and the EMG sensor measures the muscle’s electrical signal, which shows fatigue and nerve-to-muscle health. The best squeeze is kept.
  3. Compare: The software calculates the result as a percentage of the astronaut’s own baseline.
  4. Decide: The device shows a color and a recommendation.
  • Green (95% or more of baseline): stable. Keep the exercise plan, log the result, and retest next week.
  • Yellow (85–95%): declining. Add exercise time or resistance, check sleep and nutrition, and retest in one week.
  • Red (below 85%, falling fast, or early fatigue on EMG): exercise is not enough. The flight surgeon reviews the data and decides on extra treatment or an early return to Earth.

NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1 requires in-mission muscle strength to stay at or above 80% of baseline. Our 95% and 85% levels are early-warning margins above that limit.

Because the system is quick, personal, and easy to read, it offers several practical benefits to crews and mission doctors:

  • Fast and simple: five minutes a week with two small, portable tools.
  • Personal: each astronaut is compared with their own baseline, not with other people, which fits the individual differences NASA describes.
  • Early warning: the system catches decline before it reaches NASA’s 80% limit.
  • Clear decisions: a color and a recommendation instead of raw numbers.
  • Useful far from Earth: NASA notes that on deep-space missions, communication delays make it harder for ground teams to monitor crew, so a tool that gives instant guidance helps.

Our larger goal is to keep astronauts strong enough to do their jobs and to leave their vehicles in an emergency, and to let the crew and doctors adjust exercise early, before it becomes dangerous. Artemis missions to the Moon will last up to a year and Mars missions much longer, so health monitoring that works without constant help from Earth will matter more. The same approach could also help monitor muscle loss in elderly or bedridden patients on Earth.

To build the project, we used the following hardware, software, and data:

  • Hardware (proposed): handgrip dynamometer and surface EMG sensors.
  • Software: [add the tools you actually used, for example the language or app for the baseline comparison, color logic, and interface]. The logic is: current result divided by baseline, then mapped to green, yellow, or red.
  • Presentation: PowerPoint, with AI assistance for editing and formatting the slides.
  • Data: NASA/SP-20250000273, NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1, and NASA Technical Reports Server entries NTRS 20230000776 and NTRS 20110016708.

Several design choices make the project creative:

  • It combines two measurements, strength and electrical signal, to show both how strong the muscle is and how well it is working.
  • Its traffic-light output turns a medical measurement into something anyone on the crew can read in seconds.
  • It uses personal baselines instead of one standard for everyone.
  • It focuses on in-flight monitoring. NASA currently checks muscle size mainly with MRI before and after flights, and we fill the gap during the mission with a cheap, quick test.
